overview: Unit 3 introduces proof by contradiction (Widerspruchsbeweis) using the pigeonhole principle (Schubfachprinzip) and the irrationality of $\sqrt2$ (Irrationalität von √2). Contraposition (Kontraposition) and counterexamples (Gegenbeispiele) show how implications can be proved or refuted; the unit also explains labels for mathematical statements. It then covers sets (Mengen), their enumeration (Auflistung), von Neumann numbers (Von-Neumann-Zahlen), and separation and replacement (Auswahl und Ersetzung). Russell's paradox (Russellsche Antinomie) shows why set formation must be restricted to a fixed set.

entries.short: A proof by contradiction assumes the negation of the claim and derives a contradiction from it.
entries.explanation: To prove a statement $A$, first assume $\neg A$. From this assumption and the statement's hypotheses, derive consequences until an impossible statement follows. Then $\neg A$ cannot hold, so $A$ holds. The contradiction must genuinely follow from the contrary assumption and the hypotheses.
entries.example: Suppose that over 22 days, no weekday occurs four times. Then there would be at most $7\cdot3=21$ days, contradicting the 22 days under consideration.
pitfalls: A surprising consequence is not yet a contradiction.
The contradiction must follow from the contrary assumption and the hypotheses in force.
entries.heading: Widerspruchsbeweis

entries.short: If more objects are distributed than categories can accommodate at a specified maximum per category, some category must exceed that maximum.
entries.explanation: When $N$ objects are distributed among $k$ categories, at least one category contains at least $\lceil N/k\rceil$ objects. If every category contained at most $r$ objects, there would be at most $kr$ objects in total. Thus, if $N>kr$, at least one category contains more than $r$ objects.
entries.example: Among 22 days and seven weekdays, at least one weekday must occur at least four times, because $22>7\cdot3=21$.
pitfalls: The categories must cover every possible assignment of the objects.
To obtain a specific frequency bound, account for the numbers of objects and categories.
entries.heading: 22 Tage und 7 Wochentage

entries.short: Among any 22 days, at least four fall on the same weekday.
entries.explanation: The seven weekdays are the categories to which the 22 days are assigned. Under the contrary assumption that no weekday occurs four times, each weekday would occur at most three times. That would allow at most $7\cdot3=21$ days, even though 22 days are being considered. This contrary assumption leads to a contradiction.
entries.example: The days need not be consecutive; for the proof, only their assignment to one of the seven weekdays matters.
pitfalls: The claim does not require four consecutive days to fall on the same weekday.
The argument depends on the numbers of weekdays and days, not on specific calendar dates.
entries.heading: 22 Tage und 7 Wochentage

entries.term: Fraction in lowest terms (Vollständig gekürzter Bruch)
entries.short: A fraction $m/n$ is in lowest terms if $n\ne0$ and $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$.
entries.explanation: Here, $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, and the greatest common divisor is computed using the absolute values of the numerator and denominator. This condition means that the numerator and denominator have no common positive divisor other than 1. Every rational number has a representation as a fraction in lowest terms.
entries.example: $6/8$ is not in lowest terms, whereas $3/4$ is, since $\operatorname{ggT}(3,4)=1$.
pitfalls: The denominator must not be zero.
Different fractions can represent the same rational number, even though only one of them is in lowest terms.
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.term: Without loss of generality (o. B. d. A.)
entries.short: “Without loss of generality” means that a simplifying choice does not restrict the generality of the argument.
entries.explanation: The abbreviation stands for “without loss of generality.” In proving that $\sqrt2$ is irrational, one may choose a fraction in lowest terms as a hypothetical rational representation, because every rational number has such a representation. This choice simplifies the proof without excluding any possible rational representation of the number.
entries.example: The representation $6/8$ can be replaced by $3/4$ without changing the rational value it represents.
pitfalls: A simplifying assumption is valid only if the chosen representation covers every relevant case.
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.short: The number $\sqrt2$ is irrational because a representation as a fraction in lowest terms would make both numerator and denominator even.
entries.explanation: Suppose $\sqrt2=m/n$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ne0$, and $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$. Squaring gives $m^2=2n^2$, so $m^2$ is even and hence $m=2k$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. Substitution gives $n^2=2k^2$, so $n$ is also even. Thus both $m$ and $n$ are divisible by 2, contradicting $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$.
entries.example: The derivation assumes that the hypothetical rational representation is in lowest terms; this is possible because every rational number has a representation in lowest terms.
pitfalls: The implication that an integer with an even square is itself even must be justified.
The contradiction arises because both numerator and denominator are even, although their greatest common divisor is supposed to be 1.
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.short: A counterexample is a single case that refutes a general claim.
entries.explanation: For a claim intended to hold for every object in a domain, one object for which it is false is enough to refute it. For an implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, the counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis $P$ and violate the conclusion $Q$. An example in which the claim holds does not prove it in general.
entries.example: The claim “If $n^2$ is positive, then $n$ is positive” is false: for $n=-1$, $n^2=1>0$, but $n<0$.
pitfalls: For an implication, a case with a false hypothesis does not refute the implication.
A counterexample refutes a claim but does not prove another general statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: The implication $P\Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$.
entries.explanation: Thus, to prove $P\Rightarrow Q$, one can assume that $Q$ is false and show that $P$ is then false as well. The converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is not, in general, equivalent to the original implication. The contrapositive and the converse must therefore not be confused.
entries.example: To show that for integers, “$n^2$ is even” implies “$n$ is even,” prove instead: if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.
pitfalls: The converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is not the contrapositive.
The proof must use the same domain and hypotheses as the original statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: If the square of an integer is even, then the integer is even.
entries.explanation: The statement is proved by contraposition. If $n\in\mathbb Z$ is odd, there is a $k\in\mathbb Z$ such that $n=2k+1$. Then $n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$, so $n^2$ is odd. Therefore, an integer with an even square cannot be odd.
entries.example: Since $6^2=36$ is even, 6 itself is even.
pitfalls: The statement concerns integers, for which the terms even and odd apply.
The proof establishes a general implication, not merely that individual examples satisfy the statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: The proof strategy depends on the form of the statement and on whether it is to be proved or refuted.
entries.explanation: A proof by contradiction establishes a statement by deriving a contradiction from its negation. An implication can be proved directly or by proving its contrapositive. A general claim can be refuted by a suitable counterexample. These methods serve different purposes and are not freely interchangeable.
entries.example: For an implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, it may be easier to start from $\neg Q$ and derive $\neg P$.
pitfalls: A counterexample refutes a claim but does not prove another general claim.
The converse of an implication is not a substitute for its contrapositive.
entries.heading: Widerspruchsbeweis

entries.term: Labels for mathematical statements (Bezeichnungen mathematischer Aussagen)
entries.short: Labels such as definition, theorem, lemma, and corollary classify mathematical statements by their function.
entries.explanation: A definition (Def) specifies the meaning of a term. A theorem (Thm) is an important statement, while a lemma (Lem) is an auxiliary result used in a further proof. A corollary (Kor) follows directly from a theorem, and a proposition is an independent proved statement. “Fact” names a statement; the notes give Fkt as its abbreviation and remark that it is rather uncommon as a formal heading.
entries.example: A lemma can prove a subclaim that is later used in a theorem.
pitfalls: A definition specifies a meaning; it is not simply a theorem to be proved.
A heading replaces neither the statement itself nor its proof.
entries.heading: Bezeichnungen mathematischer Aussagen

entries.short: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations that must hold simultaneously.
entries.explanation: A solution is an assignment of values to the variables that satisfies every equation in the system. Variables in linear equations occur only to the first power and are not multiplied together. A system may have no solution, exactly one solution, or multiple solutions.
entries.example: The system $x+y=3$, $x-y=1$ has the solution $x=2$, $y=1$.
pitfalls: A solution must satisfy all equations simultaneously.
An equation such as $xy=1$ is not linear because it contains a product of variables.

entries.short: A set collects well-distinguished objects and is determined by its elements.
entries.explanation: For a set, what matters is whether an object belongs to it. The order and repetitions in a listing do not change the set, since $\{1,0\}=\{0,1\}=\{0,0,1\}$. Elements of a set can themselves be sets.
entries.example: $\{\mathbb N,\mathbb N_0\}$ is a set with two elements, which are themselves sets of numbers.
pitfalls: A set is not an ordered list.
An element listed more than once counts only once in a set.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The statement $x\in M$ means that $x$ is an element of the set $M$.
entries.explanation: The symbol $\in$ is read as “is an element of,” and $x\notin M$ means “is not an element of.” For every object $x$ and every set $M$, exactly one of the statements $x\in M$ or $x\notin M$ holds. The membership relation describes belonging, not order or subset inclusion.
entries.example: For $M=\{2,4\}$, we have $2\in M$ and $3\notin M$.
pitfalls: For $M=\{\{1\}\}$, we have $\{1\}\in M$, but $1\notin M$.
The membership relation $\in$ is not the same as the subset relation $\subseteq$.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The empty set $\varnothing$ contains no elements.
entries.explanation: It can be written as $\varnothing$ or as $\{\}$. For every object $x$, we have $x\notin\varnothing$. The empty set is itself a set and should therefore not be confused with an unknown value.
entries.example: In the shorthand notation used here, $[0]=\mathbb Z_0=\varnothing$.
pitfalls: $\varnothing$ and $\{\varnothing\}$ are different, because the second set contains the empty set as an element.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.term: Number sets and the axiom of infinity (Zahlenmengen und Unendlichkeitsaxiom)
entries.short: The axiom of infinity ensures an infinite set as a basis for constructing the natural numbers and further number systems.
entries.explanation: $\mathbb N_0$ denotes the natural numbers including 0, while the convention for $\mathbb N$ must be specified. The notes also use $\mathbb P$ for the prime numbers, $\mathbb Z$ for the integers, and $\mathbb R$ for the real numbers. The set $\mathbb N_0$ can be built from an infinite set; further number systems such as $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$, and $\mathbb C$ can then be constructed from it.
entries.example: $-3\in\mathbb Z$, whereas $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R$ and $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$.
pitfalls: Whether $0\in\mathbb N$ holds depends on the convention that has been specified.
Not every real number is rational.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: In an enumeration, the elements of a set are written between curly braces.
entries.explanation: We have $x\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}$ if and only if $x$ appears in the list. Strictly speaking, an enumeration must be finite and complete. Ellipses are clear when a pattern or an additional description uniquely specifies which elements are meant.
entries.example: $\{0,2,4,6\}$ lists the four even numbers from 0 to 6.
pitfalls: Ellipses without an explanatory pattern can leave it unclear which elements are meant.
Order and repetitions do not change the set being represented.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.term: Shorthand notation [n] and ℤₙ (Kurzschreibweisen [n] und ℤₙ)
entries.short: For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $[n]$ denotes the numbers from 1 to $n$, and $\mathbb Z_n$ the numbers from 0 to $n-1$.
entries.explanation: The definitions are $[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ and $\mathbb Z_n:=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$. For $n=0$, both sets are defined to be empty. This notation specifies sets by enumeration.
pitfalls: $[n]$ starts at 1, whereas $\mathbb Z_n$ starts at 0.
In this notation, $\mathbb Z_n$ denotes the listed set, not automatically arithmetic modulo $n$.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.short: The symbol $:=$ means “is defined as,” and $:gdw$ means “if and only if” in a definition.
entries.explanation: In $A:=B$, the notation on the left is specified by the expression on the right. The symbol $:gdw$ marks a definition by a condition and expresses an equivalence. Both notations make explicit that a meaning is being stipulated.
entries.example: $[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ defines the shorthand $[n]$.
pitfalls: $:=$ marks a stipulation, not merely an equality between expressions introduced earlier.
$:gdw$ denotes a two-way equivalence, not a one-way implication.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.short: The von Neumann number $\langle n\rangle$ is the set of the von Neumann numbers for the smaller natural numbers.
entries.explanation: The construction begins with $\langle0\rangle:=\varnothing$ and sets $\langle n\rangle:=\langle n-1\rangle\cup\{\langle n-1\rangle\}$ for $n\ge1$. Thus, $\langle1\rangle=\{\varnothing\}$ and $\langle2\rangle=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}$. For $m<n$, we have $\langle m\rangle\in\langle n\rangle$.
entries.example: $\langle3\rangle=\{\langle0\rangle,\langle1\rangle,\langle2\rangle\}$.
pitfalls: The natural number $n$ and its set representation $\langle n\rangle$ are different objects.
The notes mark the short relationship “$x\le y$ / $x\in y$” as unclear; what is certain in this representation is that $m<n$ implies membership $\langle m\rangle\in\langle n\rangle$.
related: Number sets and the axiom of infinity
entries.heading: Von-Neumann-Zahlen

entries.term: Rational numbers as ordered pairs (Rationale Zahlen als Zahlenpaare)
entries.short: Integers and rational numbers can be described using pairs of numbers, where different pairs can represent the same numerical value.
entries.explanation: The product $\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb N_0$ can serve as a starting point for the integers, and fractions can be described by pairs from $\mathbb Z\times(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\})$. These product sets are not, by themselves, exactly the number systems $\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Q$. A complete construction must identify pairs representing the same numerical value as equivalent; the notes do not work out these identifications.
entries.example: The pairs $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ describe the same fractional value, since $1/2=2/4$.
pitfalls: A Cartesian product is not automatically the number system whose elements the pairs represent.
Different pairs can represent the same numerical value.
related: Number sets and the axiom of infinity
entries.heading: Von-Neumann-Zahlen

entries.short: Separation selects from a fixed set exactly those elements that satisfy a given property.
entries.explanation: For a set $A$ and a property $P$, $\{y\in A\mid P(y)\}$ is the subset of elements of $A$ for which $P$ holds. We have $x\in\{y\in A\mid P(y)\}\iff x\in A\land P(x)$. The starting set limits which objects can be selected at all.
pitfalls: The property alone does not replace a fixed starting set.
The selection or separation meant here is not automatically the axiom of choice.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: Replacement collects the uniquely determined function values $f(y)$ for all $y$ in a set $A$.
entries.explanation: For a fixed set $A$ and a uniquely determined function $f$, the set $\{f(y)\mid y\in A\}$ is formed. An object $x$ belongs to it if and only if there is a $y\in A$ such that $x=f(y)$. Different inputs may yield the same function value; that value still occurs only once in the image set.
pitfalls: Exactly one function value must be determined for each input element.
Replacement collects function values, not the inputs from $A$.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: Here, a set construction is well-defined if its starting set is fixed and membership conditions or function values are uniquely determined.
entries.explanation: For separation, a fixed set $A$ must already be given, and it must be possible to determine uniquely for each element whether it satisfies the condition. For replacement, exactly one function value must also be determined for each input element. This uniquely specifies which objects belong to the resulting set.
entries.example: The selection $\{x\in\mathbb Z\mid x^2=4\}$ is well-defined and yields $\{-2,2\}$.
pitfalls: A function must assign exactly one value to each input element, but different inputs may have the same value.
An arbitrary condition over all objects, without a specified starting set, can lead to contradictions.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.term: Bound variables and conditions in set notation (Gebundene Variablen und Bedingungen in Mengenschreibweisen)
entries.short: A bound variable may be renamed consistently, and a comma between conditions means AND.
entries.explanation: In $\{x\in A\mid P(x)\}$, $x$ is bound and can be replaced by a fresh name if all occurrences are renamed consistently. A comma between conditions means that both conditions must hold at the same time. In such set expressions, a colon can be used as a separator like the vertical bar.
entries.example: $\{x\in A\mid P(x),Q(x)\}=\{x\in A\mid P(x)\land Q(x)\}$ and $\{x\in\mathbb R:|x|<1\}=\{y\in\mathbb R\mid |y|<1\}$.
pitfalls: When renaming, all occurrences of the bound variable must be replaced consistently.
A comma between conditions here means AND, not OR.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: The union contains elements from at least one of two sets, while the intersection contains only elements from both.
entries.explanation: For sets $A$ and $B$, we have $A\cup B=\{x\mid x\in A\lor x\in B\}$ and $A\cap B=\{x\mid x\in A\land x\in B\}$. Both set operations form new sets from given sets. The “or” in the union is inclusive, so an element may belong to both sets.
pitfalls: The union also contains elements that occur in both sets.
The intersection contains only elements that belong to both sets.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The unrestricted expression $R=\{x\mid x\notin x\}$ leads to a contradiction when asking whether $R\in R$.
entries.explanation:
The naive rule of forming a set of all objects satisfying any given property would allow $R=\{x\mid x
otin x\}$. If $R\in R$, the condition requires $R
otin R$; if $R
otin R$, then $R$ satisfies the condition and must therefore belong to $R$. Both possibilities lead to a contradiction. Axiomatic set theory restricts set formation, for example by using separation to select elements from a previously fixed set.
entries.example: The barber paradox poses a similar self-referential question: Does a barber who shaves exactly the men who do not shave themselves shave himself?
pitfalls: The problem arises from unrestricted set formation and self-reference, not from every ordinary finite set.
The paradox reveals a limit of naive set formation, not an ordinary contradiction in axiomatic set theory.
entries.heading: Russellsche Antinomie
